SseErrorFrame.description:
``event: error`` -- the same body an HTTP error would have carried.

Identical in shape to
:class:`~resumetailor.api.schemas.errors.ErrorEnvelope`, and deliberately
so: a streaming failure and a non-streaming one should be one thing for
the client to handle. ``error`` is the raising class's ``client_message``
and ``code`` is ``exc.code`` -- as of task 2.2 on all three routes, where
two of them previously emitted a literal that could disagree with the
exception actually raised.

This is the frame D-55 is about: it arrives inside a 200 response,
because the status line was sent before the generator produced anything.

info.description:
The ResumeTailor HTTP API.

**Errors come in three shapes.** A domain error answers `{"error", "code"}`;
an `HTTPException` raised inside a route answers `{"detail": "<sentence>"}`;
a request that fails validation before reaching a handler answers
`{"detail": [...]}`. Every documented error status lists all three, because
422 in particular can arrive as any of them. Branch on `code` where there is
one, and never on the human-readable text, which is fixed per error class and
deliberately says nothing about the inside of the server.

**The three streaming routes always answer 200.** `POST /api/resumes/stream`,
`POST /api/chat/stream` and `POST /api/evaluate/stream` send their status line
before the work starts, so a failure arrives as an `event: error` frame inside
a successful response rather than as an HTTP error status. A load balancer, an
uptime check, or any client that reads only the status line will see a
complete provider outage as 100% success. Read the frames. A client is done
with one of these responses when it has seen an `event: done` or an
`event: error` frame, not when the body ends.
info.title: ResumeTailor API

get.description:
The process is up and can answer HTTP. Touches nothing else.

Deliberately does not check the database: an orchestrator that restarts a
process on a *liveness* failure is trying to recover from a stuck or
deadlocked process, and a database outage is not that — restarting this
process fixes nothing and produces a restart loop instead. See
`/api/health/ready` for the check that does look at dependencies.

Can this process serve a real request right now.

Checks the database (a real query, not "is the file present" — D-58's
motivating case is a *corrupt* database, which opens fine and fails on the
first statement) and `PDFS_DIR` (present and writable, since every
generation ends in a write there). Both run inline rather than through
`asyncio.to_thread`: each is a handful of milliseconds and a readiness
probe that itself spawns a thread per poll is not simpler than one that
blocks the loop for a few milliseconds every few seconds.

get.description:
One page of the library.

D-10. The repository has clamped `page` and `limit` since task 1.2, so
`?limit=-1` stopped returning the whole table then; what was still missing
is that the *documented* contract said `int`, so a generated client had no
way to know the bound existed and a caller learned it by being silently
given something else. These four constraints are the same bound, declared:
an out-of-range value is now a 422 naming the field.

`sort` and `order` were the sharper half of the same gap. Both reached a
repository that turns anything other than `date` into a sort by job
description and anything other than `desc` into ascending, so `?sort=nmae`
answered 200 with a page sorted by something the caller did not ask for.
The two `Literal`s are what the frontend has always sent.

post.description:
Run the tailoring pipeline, narrating it as server-sent events.

The work is `domain.tailoring`; this handler reads what the pipeline needs,
turns each `Stage` into the progress frame the frontend expects, and hands
the result to the one function that writes it.

Wrapped in `sse_stream_tracker.track()` (task 3.5) for the whole of its
body: the lifespan's shutdown waits on this counter so a generation in
progress is not cut off mid-stream, and the same count backs
`resumetailor_sse_streams_active`. See `main.py`'s `lifespan`.

patch.description:
Rename a resume, or replace its YAML.

D-04: a write path that stores a document refuses one that will not
render, instead of storing it and surfacing the problem at render time.
The check is `resume_schema.validate` — the same schema, the same theme
and the same issue objects the renderer reports — run off the event loop
because it builds RenderCV's model.

D-57's other half is still open here: a successful YAML replacement leaves
`pdf_path` pointing at a PDF rendered from the previous document. Calling
`POST /api/resumes/{id}/render` after a PATCH is the current answer.
